summary: Describes a key exchange method for SSH in which the server proposes new groups for the Diffie-Hellman exchange to the client. The groups need not be fixed and can change over time. It is standards-track.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC adds an SSH key exchange in which the client requests a group size and the server chooses a suitable group. Both sides use that group to create a shared secret, and the server signs the exchange to authenticate itself.

questions: what is ssh diffie-hellman group exchange
what is a safe prime in ssh
why does ssh use group exchange
how does ssh choose a diffie-hellman group
subtitle: An SSH key exchange lets the server select a Diffie-Hellman group that fits the client's size request.

tldr.problem: The original SSH key exchange used one fixed Diffie-Hellman group. The RFC's authors were concerned that attackers could prepare calculations for that shared group.
tldr.mechanism: The client sends minimum, preferred, and maximum group sizes. The server selects a safe-prime group, then both sides perform the Diffie-Hellman exchange and authenticate it with the server host key.
tldr.outcome: The RFC defines SHA-1 and SHA-256 group-exchange methods and permits servers to change groups over time. RFC 4419 is updated by RFC 8270.

today: RFC 4419 is a Proposed Standard, published in March 2006, and is updated by RFC 8270. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why the Server Chooses the Group
sections.content:
SSH's original Diffie-Hellman key exchange specified one fixed group. The RFC explains that the security of Diffie-Hellman depends on the difficulty of solving a discrete logarithm, and that extensive precomputation against a fixed group could become a concern.

With group exchange, the server can prepare new groups and offer a suitable one when a client connects. The RFC presents this as a way to reduce the incentive to precompute for one group.
sections.plainLanguage: The original method made every exchange use the same group. This method lets the server offer different groups over time.

sections.title: Safe Primes and Group Sizes
sections.content:
The server keeps safe primes and corresponding generators. A prime p is safe when p = 2q + 1 and q is also prime. The generator must produce a subgroup whose order does not factor into small primes.

Clients send a minimum, preferred, and maximum group size. The RFC says clients and servers SHOULD support modulus lengths from 1024 through 8192 bits; it recommends 1024 and 8192 for the minimum and maximum request values. A returned group SHOULD be at least 1024 bits.
sections.plainLanguage: The group uses a prime with a specified mathematical structure. The client states the group sizes it can accept, and the server selects one that fits.

sections.title: The Diffie-Hellman Exchange
sections.content:
After SSH peers exchange KEXINIT messages, the client sends its minimum, preferred, and maximum group sizes. The server replies with the safe prime p and generator g. The client sends e, computed from a private random value, and the server sends f, its host key, and a signature.

Both sides compute the same shared secret and exchange hash. The client verifies the server's host key and the signature. Both sides MUST reject public values outside the specified range and accept the shared secret only when it is strictly between 1 and p - 1.
sections.plainLanguage: The client and server exchange public values and compute the same secret without sending it. The server's signature lets the client check that the exchange came from the expected host.

sections.title: Messages and Hash Algorithms
sections.content:
The exchange uses four messages: a client request, the server's group, the client's initial value, and the server's reply. The reply includes the host key, the server's public value, and a signature over an exchange hash.

The RFC defines diffie-hellman-group-exchange-sha1 and diffie-hellman-group-exchange-sha256. An older request form, message number 30, carries only the preferred size for backward compatibility; the current request carries the minimum, preferred, and maximum sizes.
sections.plainLanguage: Four messages carry the request, selected group, public values, and signed result. The method name identifies which hash algorithm the exchange uses.

sections.title: Implementation Guidance
sections.content:
The RFC recommends generator 2 because it improves multiplication performance, and it describes conditions under which it can be used. It also says a private exponent may be shortened to speed up the exchange, provided it remains at least twice as long as the key material generated from the shared secret.

The appendix gives an example method for generating a safe prime of a requested bit length. The RFC's security discussion emphasizes safe primes and explains that the security guidance for the SSH architecture also applies.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC gives choices that can make the exchange faster while preserving its stated mathematical requirements. Implementations must also follow SSH's broader security guidance.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Using multiple moduli can make precomputation against one modulus less useful. The RFC requires careful group-value checks to prevent confinement attacks and recommends using only safe primes.

A client that accepts the server's host key without verifying it leaves the protocol insecure against active attacks. The SSH architecture's security considerations apply to this key exchange as well.
sections.plainLanguage: Changing groups can limit the value of calculations prepared for one group. The client must verify the host key and both sides must check the exchanged values.
